summary.text: Today 也 means “also” or “as well” and has classical grammatical uses. A secondary report says the graph was confused with 它 after Emperor Wu of Han; the underlying paleographic argument has not been verified.

formation.text: The graph is treated as pictographic, but its pictured referent is disputed and it has no supported internal component split. The Shuowen account identifies the whole graph as female genitalia; another account identifies it as a snake. Each proposes that the sign was reused to write grammatical words because the old object-name may have sounded like those words. Neither object-name nor sound match is established. Other proposals include a crying child, a vessel or funnel, and a mouth-related form; they remain unverified here.

history.text: The selected bronze-style and seal-style forms are modern redrawings, not images of dated artifacts. The bronze-style drawing carries an uncertain period label; neither drawing establishes what the ancient graph depicted.
A secondary report says 也 was clearly distinct from 它 in early scripts and that the two became confused only after Emperor Wu of Han. Its underlying paleographic argument has not been verified.

uncertainties.text: The original referent and earliest securely documented occurrence of the graph remain unresolved. The proposed connection with 啼 is reported through a secondary summary; the underlying paleographic argument was not inspected.
The two proposed borrowing accounts cannot be checked against the pictured object’s name or pronunciation, which are not established.
The evidence does not establish a chronological order or semantic path among particle, copular-like, affirmative, focus, and “also” uses.

senses.text: 也 has classical grammatical uses. The earliest securely dated occurrence is unsettled; general glosses and transmitted examples do not establish it.
Modern Chinese uses 也 as an adverb meaning “also” or “as well.” Dictionary glosses attest the use but do not establish when or how it developed from particle uses.

senses.period: pre-Qin texts; precise dating unresolved here
senses.text: A grammatical analysis identifies copular use in the Guodian corpus and proposes a path from focus particle to copula. This concerns the word’s grammatical use, not the graph’s origin, and does not establish a dated sequence here.

limitations.text: The evidence does not establish chronology among particle, copular-like, affirmative, focus, and “also” uses, so no semantic-development links are asserted.

The Shuowen commentary and a character database propose that the graph was borrowed for function words. The object-name and pronunciation behind the proposed pictures are not established, so the proposed sound matches cannot be checked.
Comparisons with Tibetan and 唯 are reported as hypotheses; their primary arguments and sound correspondences are not established here.

overview.text: Today 也 means “also” or “as well.” Proposed picture origins include female genitalia and a snake; the old object-name and sound match that might explain reuse for grammatical words are not established.
